# nish/array

The array methods that take a callback, and `slice`, in Nish: each a plain loop, compiled once per callback.

```ts
import {
  every,
  everyIndexed,
  filter,
  filterIndexed,
  findIndex,
  findIndexIndexed,
  forEach,
  forEachIndexed,
  map,
  mapIndexed,
  slice,
  sliceAll,
  sliceFrom,
  some,
  someIndexed,
} from "nish/array";
```

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
export const main = (): i32 => {
  const xs: i32[] = [3, 1, 2];
  const doubled = xs.map((x) => x * 2); // [6, 2, 4]
  const big = xs.filter((x) => x > 1); // [3, 2]
  return doubled[0] + big.length + xs.findIndex((x) => x === 2); // 6 + 2 + 2
};
```

</scalar-code-group>

<scalar-detail title="A program does not need to import this module">

A `.map(...)`,
`.filter(...)`, `.some(...)`, `.every(...)`, `.findIndex(...)`,
`.forEach(...)` or `.slice(...)` call on an array is what loads it (the checker's
`importArrayMethods`), and the checker routes the call to the template here
that matches it: `xs.map(f)` is `map(xs, f)` when `f` takes one parameter
and `mapIndexed(xs, f)` when it takes two. `f` is a compile-time function
parameter, so each callback is an instantiation of its own whose body calls
it directly — there is no function pointer, and importing a template here
by name and calling it gives the same code as the method. Under Node,
`--emit-ts` leaves `map`, `filter`, `some`, `every`, `findIndex` and
`forEach` as the
platform's own `Array.prototype` methods, writes `slice` as the runtime's
checked `sliceArray`, and copies an answer that holds records inline with
`copyRecords`, so nothing here runs there.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Same answers as Node">

Each walks the array from index 0 upward and
calls the callback once per element, in order, until the length it had when
the call began, as `Array.prototype` does; `some`, `every` and `findIndex`
stop at the first element that decides the answer. A callback that shrinks
the array ends the walk at the new length, where JavaScript goes on and
skips the missing indices.

</scalar-detail>

## Functions

### every

Whether `pred` answers `true` for every element of `xs`, stopping at the
first that does not: what `xs.every(pred)` compiles to when `pred` takes one
parameter. An empty array answers `true`.

```ts
function every<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  pred: (x: T) => boolean,
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="pred" type="(x: T) =&gt; boolean" required>

called in order until it answers `false`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

`true` when no element fails `pred`.

</scalar-field>

### everyIndexed

Whether `pred` answers `true` for every element of `xs`, given each element
and its index: what `xs.every(pred)` compiles to when `pred` takes two
parameters.

```ts
function everyIndexed<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  pred: (x: T, i: number) => boolean,
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="pred" type="(x: T, i: number) =&gt; boolean" required>

called in order, with the element and its index, until it answers `false`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

`true` when no element fails `pred`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

### forEach

Calls `f` with each element of `xs`, in order: what `xs.forEach(f)`
compiles to when `f` takes one parameter. The walk stops at the length the
array had when the call began, so an element the callback pushes is not
visited, and at the current length, so one it pops is not either, as
`Array.prototype.forEach` does.

```ts
function forEach<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  f: (x: T) => void,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; the callback may change it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(x: T) =&gt; void" required>

called once per element, in order.

</scalar-field>

### forEachIndexed

Calls `f` with each element of `xs` and its index, in order: what
`xs.forEach(f)` compiles to when `f` takes two parameters. The walk stops
where `forEach`'s does.

```ts
function forEachIndexed<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  f: (x: T, i: number) => void,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; the callback may change it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(x: T, i: number) =&gt; void" required>

called once per element, in order, with the element and its index.

</scalar-field>

### map

The elements of `xs`, each passed through `f`, in a new array of the same
length: what `xs.map(f)` compiles to when `f` takes one parameter.

```ts
function map<T, U>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  f: (x: T) => U,
): U[]
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(x: T) =&gt; U" required>

called once per element, in order.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="U[]">

a new array whose element `i` is `f(xs[i])`.

</scalar-field>

### mapIndexed

The elements of `xs`, each passed through `f` with its index: what
`xs.map(f)` compiles to when `f` takes two parameters.

```ts
function mapIndexed<T, U>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  f: (x: T, i: number) => U,
): U[]
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="f" type="(x: T, i: number) =&gt; U" required>

called once per element, in order, with the element and its index.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="U[]">

a new array whose element `i` is `f(xs[i], i)`.

</scalar-field>

### slice

A copy of `xs[start..end)` in a new array: what `xs.slice(start, end)`
compiles to, with string `slice`'s rule. The range must satisfy
`0 <= start <= end <= xs.length`, and anything else panics with
`slice out of range: [start, end) of length n` and exits 1, where
JavaScript counts a negative end back from the length and clamps the rest.
A float bound is truncated toward zero and saturates (NaN to 0, an infinity
to the `i64` limit), natively and under Node alike.

```ts
function slice<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  start: number,
  end: number,
): T[]
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array copied from; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="start" type="number" required>

the first index copied.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="end" type="number" required>

the index after the last copied.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="T[]">

a new array of `end - start` elements.

</scalar-field>

### sliceAll

A copy of the whole of `xs`: what `xs.slice()` compiles to.

```ts
function sliceAll<T>(xs: readonly T[]): T[]
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array copied; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="T[]">

a new array with the same elements.

</scalar-field>

### sliceFrom

A copy of `xs[start..)`: what `xs.slice(start)` compiles to. `start` must
satisfy `0 <= start <= xs.length`, or the call panics as `slice` does.

```ts
function sliceFrom<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  start: number,
): T[]
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array copied from; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="start" type="number" required>

the first index copied.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="T[]">

a new array of the elements from `start` on.

</scalar-field>

### some

Whether `pred` answers `true` for at least one element of `xs`, stopping at
the first that does: what `xs.some(pred)` compiles to when `pred` takes one
parameter. An empty array answers `false`.

```ts
function some<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  pred: (x: T) => boolean,
): boolean
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

the array read; it is not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="pred" type="(x: T) =&gt; boolean" required>

called in order until it answers `true`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="boolean">

`true` when some element satisfies `pred`.

</scalar-field>

### someIndexed

Whether `pred` answers `true` for at least one element of `xs`, given each
element and its index: what `xs.some(pred)` compiles to when `pred` takes
two parameters.

```ts
function someIndexed<T>(
  xs: readonly T[],
  pred: (x: T, i: number) => boolean,
```

<scalar-field name="xs" type="readonly T[]" required>

<scalar-field name="pred" type="(x: T, i: number) =&gt; boolean" required>
